Greedy
gree'dy
a. (ravenous, insatiable; in the Authorized Version chiefly greedy of gain and greedy of filthy lucre, a disqualification for office)
Old English graedig, hungry or covetous. The Hebrew idiom at Proverbs 1:19 is botsea batsa, one who cuts off gain by violence; the Greek at 1 Timothy 3:3 is aischrokerdes, eager for shameful profit.

Biblical Definition

Scripture almost never uses greedy of the stomach; it uses it of gain. “So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof” (Proverbs 1:19) — the Hebrew pictures a man cutting off a profit by violence, and the proverb notes that the profit destroys the one who takes it. The household consequence is stated plainly: “He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live” (Proverbs 15:27). Isaiah turns the word on shepherds, which is to say on ministers: “Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain” (Isaiah 56:11). Paul takes it up as a formal disqualification for church office in both lists — an overseer must be “not greedy of filthy lucre” (1 Timothy 3:3), and so must a deacon (1 Timothy 3:8). The Greek aischrokerdes names not the amount but the appetite: money loved for itself, sought in ways that shame the seeker. The word describes a settled orientation of the heart, which is why it bars a man from office rather than merely calling for his correction.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines greedy as having a keen appetite, ravenous, and figuratively as eager to obtain, especially of money.

expand to see more

GREEDY, a. Having a keen appetite for food or drink; ravenous; voracious; very hungry.

2. Having a keen desire for any thing; eager to obtain; as greedy of gain.

They are greedy dogs which can never have enough.

GREEDINESS, n. Keenness of appetite for food or drink; ravenousness; voracity.

2. Ardent desire; as greediness of gain.

Key Scripture

Proverbs 1:19 — "So are the ways of every one that is greedy of gain; which taketh away the life of the owners thereof."

Proverbs 15:27 — "He that is greedy of gain troubleth his own house; but he that hateth gifts shall live."

Isaiah 56:11 — "Yea, they are greedy dogs which can never have enough, and they are shepherds that cannot understand: they all look to their own way, every one for his gain, from his quarter."

1 Timothy 3:8 — "Likewise must the deacons be grave, not doubletongued, not given to much wine, not greedy of filthy lucre;"

Modern Corruption

Greed has been reclassified as ambition and rebranded a virtue, while the specific disqualification of a greedy minister is quietly ignored.

expand to see more

In the commercial register greed has been laundered into drive, hunger, or ambition, and it is now praised in the same terms Isaiah uses to condemn: a man who can never have enough. Scripture does not object to profit, to industry, or to wealth honestly gotten; Abraham, Job, and Boaz were all rich men. It objects to the appetite that makes gain the end, and it says twice what that appetite costs — it takes away the life of the owner, and it troubles his own house. Proverbs 15:27 sets the antidote in the second clause: he that hateth gifts shall live. The bribe refused is the mark of the man not ruled by gain.

The graver corruption is inside the church, and Isaiah aimed at it first. Greedy dogs are shepherds; the men who cannot have enough are ministers. Paul made freedom from that appetite a condition of holding office — not an area for growth, a condition — and the modern church has largely stopped applying it. Where a ministry is structured so that the preacher's income rises with the intensity of his appeals, 1 Timothy 3:3 has been suspended in practice however loudly it is affirmed on paper. The apostolic remedy was structural: Paul would not handle the collection alone, and he worked with his own hands rather than be chargeable to any.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew botsea batsa, one greedy of unjust gain — Proverbs 1:19, 15:27; az nephesh, strong of appetite — Isaiah 56:11; Greek aischrokerdes, eager for base gain — 1 Timothy 3:8.

expand to see more

Hebrew batsa — to cut off, to gain by violence; the noun is unjust profit, Proverbs 1:19.

Hebrew az nephesh — strong of soul or appetite; Isaiah 56:11, of shepherds who can never have enough.

Greek aischrokerdes — greedy of shameful gain; 1 Timothy 3:8 and Titus 1:7, both office qualifications.

Greek pleonexia — the desire to have more; Colossians 3:5, where it is named idolatry.

Old English graedig — hungry, covetous; the root of the English word.

Usage

"“Greedy of gain” — the Authorized Version's standing phrase, and it takes the owner's life."

"“Greedy dogs which can never have enough” — Isaiah's verdict on hireling shepherds."

"“Not greedy of filthy lucre” — a bar to office, not a matter for improvement."
